content: 1. Individuals affected by leprosy play a critical role in leprosy control programs. Their involvement is essential for facilitating early diagnosis, improving access to care, and ensuring better treatment adherence. 2. Strategies should aim to empower individuals affected by leprosy by building their capacity in advocacy and establishing networks for psycho-social support. This approach helps reduce emotional and economic distress, which often leads to depression and poverty. 3. Persons affected by leprosy can contribute significantly to early identification of cases and adherence to treatment regimens. Their participation enhances the effectiveness of leprosy services. 4. International, national, and local organizations representing individuals affected by leprosy are integral to the success of these initiatives. Their collaboration ensures a comprehensive approach to leprosy control. 5. Promoting equity and social justice in all aspects of service provision for patients, their families, and communities is a priority. This includes addressing stigma and discrimination through partnerships with non-governmental and civil society organizations. 6. The Human Rights Council of the United Nations adopted Resolution 29/5 on July 2, 2015, titled Elimination of discrimination against persons affected by leprosy and their family members. This resolution underscores the importance of protecting the human rights of those affected by the disease. 7. Research efforts should focus on understanding leprosy transmission, developing new diagnostic tools, prophylactic regimens, and innovative therapeutics. Operational research should involve all stakeholders to identify and implement effective strategies and interventions. 8. The integration of leprosy control within neglected tropical disease (NTD) programs should be assessed to ensure its effectiveness. Establishing linkages among research bodies, funding agencies, programs, universities, public laboratories, patient groups, and regulators is essential for advancing research and integrating findings into leprosy programs. 9. Strengthening government ownership, coordination, and partnerships is vital for leprosy control. This includes ensuring political commitment, adequate resources, and collaboration with state and non-state actors at both national and international levels. 10. Efforts to stop leprosy and its complications should include raising awareness in high-endemic areas, ensuring prompt treatment initiation and adherence, improving disability prevention and management, and strengthening surveillance for antimicrobial resistance. 11. Innovative approaches, such as eHealth, should be promoted for training, referrals, and sustaining expertise in leprosy management. Interventions to prevent infection and disease should also be prioritized. 12. Addressing discrimination and promoting inclusion are key to societal integration. This involves empowering individuals affected by leprosy, involving communities in service improvement, and supporting community-based rehabilitation for those with leprosy-related disabilities. 13. Regional and country-specific implementation plans should provide practical recommendations for core leprosy services. These plans should be developed, discussed, and disseminated to ensure effective action. 14. Monitoring of targets and indicators, such as the number of new child cases with Grade 2 disabilities (G2D), is crucial for tracking progress toward eliminating leprosy as a public health problem. Surveillance for drug resistance should be expanded, and data recording and reporting systems should be modernized. 15. Tools to monitor stigma and the impact of activities aimed at reducing it should be developed and promoted through training and supervision. Research on disease modeling to compare expected and observed trends should be encouraged. 16. Advocacy for the Global Leprosy Strategy should focus on increasing acceptance among national programs and stakeholders. Modern communication strategies should be developed to raise community awareness about leprosy. 17. The WHO Global Leprosy Programme will enhance its Technical Advisory Group (TAG) to include representation from national programs and individuals affected by leprosy. This will ensure broader support for implementing the new strategy. 18. The Global Leprosy Strategy 2016–2020, titled Accelerating towards a leprosy-free world, was developed through consultations with various stakeholders, including national programs, technical agencies, public health experts, funding agencies, and representatives of affected communities. 19. The strategy focuses on three pillars: strengthening government ownership and partnerships, stopping leprosy and its complications, and stopping discrimination while promoting inclusion. Its goals include achieving zero children with leprosy-related disabilities, reducing new cases with deformities to less than one per million population, and repealing discriminatory laws. 20. The strategy was endorsed by the WHO Technical Advisory Group on leprosy, reflecting its importance in reducing the global and local burden of the disease.
